name: Pashto
where: Afghanistan (official language, alongside Dari) and Pakistan (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, northern Balochistan, the former tribal areas, and large communities in Karachi); diaspora in the Gulf, UK, Germany and North America
tagline: The proud, poetic language of the Pashtuns — learn it and every door in the mountains from Kandahar to Peshawar opens with a cup of green tea.
intro:
**Pashto** (پښتو, *paṣtó*) is an Eastern Iranian language, a distant cousin of Persian and Kurdish, spoken by the Pashtun people on both sides of the Afghanistan–Pakistan border. It is one of the two official languages of Afghanistan and the largest regional language of Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Pashto has a rich oral and written literature — the 17th-century poet-warrior **Khushal Khan Khattak**, the Sufi poet **Rahman Baba**, and the two-line folk poems called *landay* that every Pashtun knows by heart.

Pashto is written right to left in its own extension of the Perso-Arabic alphabet, with letters for sounds Persian and Urdu do not have: the retroflexes ټ ډ ړ ڼ, the affricates څ ځ, the sounds ښ ږ, and a whole set of word-final letters (ی ي ې ۍ ئ) that carry grammar — gender, number and person.

There are two main dialect groups. The **'soft' southern** dialects (Kandahar and the south-west, also the basis of the literary standard) pronounce ښ as a curled-tongue *sh* and ږ as a curled-tongue *zh*; the **'hard' northern** dialects (Peshawar, Mardan, Swat — the Yusufzai area) pronounce ښ as *x* (like خ) and ږ as *g*. That is why the language itself is called *Pashto* in Kandahar and *Pakhto* in Peshawar. Everyone understands both. This course teaches the standard soft pronunciation used in education and broadcasting, and points out the Peshawar pronunciation wherever it differs.

Pashto grammar has a reputation: nouns change for **case** (direct, oblique, vocative), verbs have **perfective and imperfective aspect** (usually marked by the prefix و- *wə́-*), small **clitic pronouns** (مې دې يې مو) slip into second position in the sentence, and in the past tense the language is **ergative** — 'I ate the bread' becomes 'by me the bread was eaten'. It sounds hard, but it is beautifully systematic, and this course introduces each piece slowly, one unit at a time.
romanizationNote: The romanization shows the standard 'soft' pronunciation. Vowels: **a** is short (the 'u' of 'cup'), **ā** long as in 'father', **ə** is the short neutral 'uh' of 'about' (very common in Pashto: زه zə 'I'), **i** as in 'sit' or 'see', **u** as in 'put' or 'rule' (Pashto does not distinguish long and short i/u, so no bars are used for them), **e** as in 'café', **o** as in 'go'; **ay** (ی) is like 'eye' cut short, **əy** (ۍ ئ) is 'uh' + y, **aw** like 'cow'. Consonants: **ṭ ḍ ṇ** are retroflex (tongue curled back), **ṛ** is a retroflex flap that can sound halfway between r and l; plain **t d** are dental (tongue on the teeth). **ts** (څ) as in 'cats', **dz** (ځ) as in 'adze'; **x** (خ) as in Scottish 'loch', **ġ** (غ) a gargled g, **q** (ق) a k far back in the throat; **ch** (چ), **j** (ج), **sh** (ش), **zh** (ژ, the s of 'measure'); **ṣ** (ښ) and **ẓ** (ږ) are sh and zh said with the tongue curled back — in Peshawar/Yusufzai Pashto ṣ is pronounced x and ẓ is pronounced g. Pashto has no aspirated consonants, so k p t never have a puff of air, and **kh** is never used. **ʿ** (ع) and **’** (ء) appear in Arabic loanwords and are usually silent. **Stress** is shown with an acute accent (á ā́ ə́ é í ó ú) where it matters — above all in verbs, where the stressed perfective prefix **wə́-** and the place of the stress can change the meaning (راوړم rāwṛə́m 'I was bringing' vs rā́wṛəm 'I brought'). Where no accent is shown, stressing the last syllable of the stem is a safe default.

script.overview:
Pashto is written **right to left** in an alphabet of **44 letters**, based on Arabic and Persian with extra letters for Pashto sounds. The extra letters are made by adding marks to familiar shapes: a small ring (*ġwanḍəy*, 'little circle') under ت د ر ن gives the retroflexes **ټ ډ ړ ڼ**; three dots or a hamza on ح gives **څ** (ts) and **ځ** (dz); a dot above and below gives **ښ** and **ږ**; and Pashto **ګ** (g) has a ring at the bottom instead of the Persian/Urdu double stroke (گ). The everyday print style is upright **Naskh**, which is what this course uses.

The script is cursive: most letters join to the letter before **and** after them, so they have up to four shapes (isolated, initial, medial, final). **Eleven letters never join to the following letter**: ا آ د ډ ذ ر ړ ز ژ ږ و. After one of these the next letter starts a new chunk, even inside a word — so ورور (wror, brother) is written as four separate pieces.

Like Persian and Urdu, Pashto writing shows consonants and long vowels but usually leaves out short vowels. The difference is that Pashto spells **word endings** very precisely: there are five different 'ye' letters at the end of a word (ی ay, ي i, ې e, ۍ əy, ئ əy) and final ه can be -a or -ə. These endings tell you the gender, number, case and person of a word, so they are the most important spelling skill in Pashto. In Pakistan you will also see ۀ (he with hamza) for final -ə and کښې for کې ('in').

Short vowels can be marked with diacritics — *zwar* (a), *zer* (i), *pesh* (u) and the special Pashto **zwarakay** (ə) — but ordinary books and newspapers rarely use them. Numbers use Eastern Arabic-Indic digits in their Persian forms (۰ ۱ ۲ ۳ ۴ ۵ ۶ ۷ ۸ ۹), written left to right even inside right-to-left text.

groups.title: Alif and the 'be' family
groups.note: Alif is a non-connector. ب پ ت ټ ث share one 'boat' shape and differ only in their dots or ring; in the middle of a word each is just a small tooth.

letters.sound: alif. At the start of a word it carries a short vowel (a, ə, i, u); elsewhere it is long ā as in 'father'. Non-connector: never joins to the next letter (final form ـا).
letters.strokes: One straight stroke from top to bottom.

letters.sound: alif madd: long ā at the start of a word. Non-connector.
letters.strokes: Alif with a wavy madd stroke on top.

letters.sound: be. Like English b. Joins both ways: بـ ـبـ ـب.
letters.strokes: A shallow boat drawn right to left; one dot below.

letters.sound: pe. Like p in 'spin' — no puff of air. Joins both ways: پـ ـپـ ـپ.
letters.strokes: The boat with three dots below.

letters.sound: te. A dental t: tongue tip against the back of the upper teeth, no puff of air. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The boat with two dots above.

letters.sound: ṭe. Retroflex t: curl the tongue tip back to the roof of the mouth. Pashto letter. Joins both ways: ټـ ـټـ ـټ.
letters.strokes: The boat with a small ring (ġwanḍəy) above.

letters.sound: se. Pronounced s; only in Arabic loanwords. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The boat with three dots above.

groups.title: The 'jim' family
groups.note: Six letters on one hook shape. ځ and څ are Pashto letters for the sounds dz and ts. All join both ways; initial and medial forms lose the tail (جـ ـجـ).

letters.sound: jim. Like j in 'jam'.
letters.strokes: A cap stroke to the left, then a deep hook down and round; one dot inside.

letters.sound: dze. dz as in 'adze' or 'kids'. Pashto letter. In Yusufzai/Peshawar speech often plain z.
letters.strokes: The hook with a small hamza (ء) inside instead of a dot.

letters.sound: che. Like ch in 'church'.
letters.strokes: The hook with three dots inside.

letters.sound: tse. ts as in 'cats'. Pashto letter. In Yusufzai/Peshawar speech often plain s.
letters.strokes: The hook with three dots above it (not inside).

letters.sound: he (hā-ye hutti). Pronounced like ordinary h; Arabic loanwords only.
letters.strokes: The plain hook with no dot.

letters.sound: xe. The rough sound of Scottish 'loch' or German 'Bach'.
letters.strokes: The hook with one dot above.

groups.title: The 'dal' family (non-connectors)
groups.note: These never join to the following letter.

letters.sound: dāl. Dental d: tongue on the back of the upper teeth. Also the very common word د (də) 'of'.
letters.strokes: A small angle: short stroke down-left, then along to the left.

letters.sound: ḍāl. Retroflex d: tongue tip curled back. Pashto letter.
letters.strokes: دال with a small ring below its foot.

letters.sound: zāl. Pronounced z; Arabic loanwords only.
letters.strokes: دال with one dot above.

groups.title: The 're' family (non-connectors)
groups.note: Five letters on one short curved shape that dips below the line. ړ and ږ are Pashto letters. None joins to the following letter.

letters.sound: re. A tapped or lightly rolled r, as in Spanish 'pero'.
letters.strokes: A short curve dropping below the line to the left.

letters.sound: ṛe. Retroflex flap: curl the tongue back and flick it forward — to English ears it sounds between r, d and l. Pashto letter.
letters.strokes: ر with a small ring above.

letters.sound: ze. Like English z.
letters.strokes: ر with one dot above.

letters.sound: zhe. The s in 'measure'.
letters.strokes: ر with three dots above.

letters.sound: ẓe. Soft dialects: zh with the tongue curled back. Peshawar/Yusufzai: g (so موږ muẓ 'we' is heard as 'mung/mug'). Pashto letter.
letters.strokes: ر with one dot above and one below.

groups.title: The 'sin', 'swād' and 'toy' families
groups.note: Three-toothed س family (س ش ښ), the loop-shaped ص ض, and the upright ط ظ. All join both ways. ص ض ط ظ appear only in Arabic loanwords.

letters.sound: sin. Like English s.
letters.strokes: Three small teeth and then a deep bowl.

letters.sound: shin. Like sh in 'ship'.
letters.strokes: س with three dots above.

letters.sound: ṣin. Soft dialects: sh with the tongue tip curled back (between 'sh' and 's'). Peshawar/Yusufzai: x as in 'loch' (پښتو → Pakhto). Pashto letter.
letters.strokes: س with one dot above and one dot below.

letters.sound: swād. Pronounced s.
letters.strokes: A flat loop, then a bowl.

letters.sound: zwād. Pronounced z.
letters.strokes: ص with one dot above.

letters.sound: toy. Pronounced t (dental).
letters.strokes: A flat loop with a tall upright stroke.

letters.sound: zoy. Pronounced z.
letters.strokes: ط with one dot.

groups.title: The 'ayn', 'fe' and 'qāf' families
groups.note: ع and غ change shape a lot: initial عـ غـ, medial ـعـ ـغـ (a small closed triangle), final ـع ـغ.

letters.sound: ayn. In Pashto usually silent or a slight catch in the voice; it just carries the vowel. Arabic loanwords only.
letters.strokes: An open 'c' shape on top and a bowl below.

letters.sound: ġayn. A gargled g, the voiced partner of خ (like French r in 'Paris').
letters.strokes: ع with one dot above.

letters.sound: fe. Like f. In some rural speech replaced by p.
letters.strokes: A small round loop on a boat; one dot above.

letters.sound: qāf. A k made far back in the throat; many speakers say plain k.
letters.strokes: Loop with a deeper round bowl; two dots above.

groups.title: kāf, gāf, lām, mim, nun and ṇun
groups.note: Pashto ګ is written with a little ring at the bottom, not the double stroke of Persian/Urdu گ. All of these join both ways.

letters.sound: kāf. k as in 'skin' — no puff of air. Initial/medial کـ ـکـ.
letters.strokes: A tall slanted stroke with a flat base; a small hamza-like mark inside when isolated.

letters.sound: gāf. Hard g as in 'go'. Pashto spelling has a small ring at the bottom (ګ), not گ.
letters.strokes: کاف shape with a small ring under its base.

letters.sound: lām. A clear l. With alif it forms the ligature لا (lā).
letters.strokes: A tall upright stroke curving into a bowl.

letters.sound: mim. Like m. Initial مـ, medial ـمـ are a small round head.
letters.strokes: A small round loop with a tail down.

letters.sound: nun. Dental n; before k/g it sounds like ng.
letters.strokes: A round bowl with one dot above.

letters.sound: ṇun. Retroflex n, tongue curled back. Pashto letter; never at the start of a word.
letters.strokes: ن with a small ring under the bowl (no dot when final in careful print: ـڼ).

groups.title: wāw, he and hamza
groups.note: و is both a consonant (w) and a vowel letter (o, u). ه is h at the start of a syllable, but at the end of a word it is the vowel -a or -ə.

letters.sound: wāw. Consonant w (Pashto has no v sound in native words), or the vowels o / u. Also the word و (aw) 'and'. Non-connector.
letters.strokes: A small round head on a tail that dips below the line.

letters.sound: he. At the start of a syllable: h. At the end of a word: the vowel -a (most feminine nouns: ښځه ṣədzá) or -ə (زه zə). Four forms: هـ ـهـ ـه ه. Pakistani spelling often writes final -ə as ۀ.
letters.strokes: Isolated: a small round loop; initial: a loop with an inner stroke; final: a small hooked loop.

letters.sound: hamza. A glottal catch, mostly in Arabic loanwords; often just separates two vowels. Sits on its own or on a ye-seat (ئـ).
letters.strokes: A small '2'-like mark.

groups.title: The five ye's (word endings that carry grammar)
groups.note: In the middle of a word all of these look the same (يـ ـيـ). At the end of a word they are five different letters with five different jobs — learn them carefully.

letters.sound: nārina ye ('masculine ye'), no dots. At the end of a word = -ay: the typical ending of masculine nouns and adjectives (سړی saṛáy 'man', ستړی stə́ṛay 'tired (m)'), and the copula دی day 'is (m)'.
letters.strokes: A deep reversed-S curve with no dots.

letters.sound: ma'rufa ye, two dots below. Consonant y at the start of a syllable; vowel i. At the end of a word = -i: masculine plurals (سړي saṛí 'men'), oblique of -ay nouns, and the 3rd-person verb ending (کوي kawí 'does').
letters.strokes: The ye curve with two dots side by side below.

letters.sound: majhula ye, two dots one above the other. At the end of a word = -e: feminine plurals (ښځې ṣədzé 'women'), feminine oblique, the 2nd-person singular verb ending (ته ځې tə dze 'you go'), and the words کې ke 'in', دې de.
letters.strokes: The ye curve with two dots stacked vertically below.

letters.sound: ṣədzína ye ('feminine ye'), with a small tail. Only at the end of a word = -əy: feminine nouns and adjectives like نجلۍ njlə́y 'girl', ډوډۍ ḍoḍə́y 'bread', لومړۍ lumṛə́y 'first (f)'.
letters.strokes: The dotless ye with a short stroke (hamza-like tail) on its end.

letters.sound: fe'liya ye ('verbal ye'), ye with hamza. At the end of a word = -əy: the 2nd-person plural / polite verb ending (تاسو ځئ tāso dzəy 'you go') and imperatives (کېنئ kénəy 'sit down'). In the middle of loanwords it is a hamza seat.
letters.strokes: Dotless ye with a small hamza (ء) above it.

groups.title: Writing vowels
groups.note: Pashto has nine vowel sounds: a ā ə i u e o plus the endings ay and əy. Long or 'full' vowels are written with letters; short a, ə, i, u are usually not written inside a word. At the start of a word a vowel needs alif as its carrier.

letters.sound: Short a, like u in 'cup'. Usually not written (zwar).
letters.strokes: Alif with a slanted stroke above.

letters.sound: Long ā, like 'father' (often rounded, towards 'law'). آ at the start of a word, ا elsewhere.
letters.strokes: Alif (with madd at the beginning of a word).

letters.sound: Schwa, the neutral 'uh' of 'about'. Inside a word usually unwritten (zwarakay ◌ٙ in careful texts); at the end of a word written ه (زه zə, په pə).
letters.strokes: Alif with a small zwarakay mark above.

letters.sound: i as in 'sit' or 'see' (length is not important). Written ي inside or at the end of a word, or left unwritten.
letters.strokes: Alif + ye (two dots below).

letters.sound: u as in 'put' or 'rule'. Written و, or left unwritten.
letters.strokes: Alif + wāw.

letters.sound: e as in 'café'. Written ې at the end of a word and ـېـ inside it (dots stacked).
letters.strokes: Alif + ye with two stacked dots.

letters.sound: o as in 'go' (a pure vowel). Written و.
letters.strokes: Alif + wāw.

letters.sound: Diphthong ay as in 'eye' — only written ی at the end of a word; inside a word ـيـ.
letters.strokes: Alif + dotless ye.

letters.sound: əy, 'uh' gliding to y — ۍ for feminine nouns/adjectives, ئ for verb endings.
letters.strokes: Ye with a little tail (ۍ) or a hamza (ئ).

groups.title: Diacritics and punctuation
groups.note: Small marks above and below the letters. Everyday Pashto leaves most of them out; dictionaries, schoolbooks and religious texts use them.

letters.sound: zwar (Arabic fatha): short a.
letters.strokes: A short slanting stroke above.

letters.sound: zer (kasra): short i.
letters.strokes: A short slanting stroke below.

letters.sound: pesh (damma): short u.
letters.strokes: A tiny wāw above.

letters.sound: zwarakay ('little zwar'): the Pashto mark for the schwa ə. Rare in print, but shows you the vowel in words like ښٙځه ṣədzá.
letters.strokes: A small inverted v or tick above the letter.

letters.sound: jazm / sukun: no vowel follows. Useful for Pashto's initial clusters: سْپين spin, not 'sapin'.
letters.strokes: A small circle above.

letters.sound: shadd / tashdid: the consonant is doubled. Mostly in Arabic loans.
letters.strokes: A small 'w' above.

letters.sound: tanwin: final -an in Arabic adverbs.
letters.strokes: Two zwar strokes over alif.

letters.sound: he with hamza: in Pakistani (and older Afghan) spelling marks final -ə, to tell it apart from final -a: زۀ zə 'I', but ښځه ṣədzá 'woman'. This course uses the Afghan standard ه.
letters.strokes: Final he with a small hamza above.

letters.sound: Question mark, mirror-image. The comma is ، and the semicolon ؛; the full stop is a plain dot (.) in Afghan print or ۔ in Pakistani print.
letters.strokes: A reversed question mark.

groups.title: Joining in practice
groups.note: Real words showing how letters connect — and where non-connectors break a word into pieces.

letters.sound: پـ + ـښـ + ـتـ + ـو: three connecting letters, then non-connector و ends the word. Pronounced 'Pakhto' in Peshawar.
و · ر · و · ر — four non-connectors, so four separate pieces.
lām + alif always fuse into the ligature لا.
ښـ + ـځـ + ـه: initial, medial and final forms; final ه = -a (feminine).
کـ + ـړ (non-connector, breaks the word) + کـ + ـۍ.
ډ is a non-connector; then ېـ in its medial form (two stacked dots) joins to ر.

groups.title: Digits ۰–۹
groups.note: Pashto uses the Persian forms of the Eastern Arabic-Indic digits. Numbers are written left to right: ۲۵ = 25. Western digits are also common, especially in Pakistan.

letters.sound: sifr (zero): a small dot.
yaw: a vertical stroke.
dwa: a stroke with one hook at the top.
dre: a stroke with two hooks at the top.
tsalór: Persian form with a loop (not the Arabic ٤).
pindzə: an upside-down heart / round loop (not the Arabic ٥).
shpaẓ: Persian form with a tail to the left (not ٦).
owə: a V shape.
atə: an upside-down V.
nəhə: a small loop on a stem.

pronunciation.title: Retroflex ټ ډ ړ ڼ vs dental ت د ر ن
pronunciation.body:
Pashto, like Urdu, has two sets of t/d/n sounds. The **dental** ones (ت د ن) are made with the tongue tip touching the back of the upper front teeth — further forward than English t, d, n. The **retroflex** ones (ټ ډ ڼ) are made by curling the tongue tip back and striking the hard ridge behind the gums — further back than English. English t and d fall in between, so English speakers have to move in both directions.

**ړ** is the hardest: a retroflex flap. Curl the tongue back and flick it forward and down as you say the vowel. To English ears it can sound like r, d or even l. It is everywhere in Pashto: سړی saṛáy 'man', زړه zṛə 'heart', وړوکی waṛúkay 'small'. All four retroflex letters are written with the little ring (ġwanḍəy).
tips: For ت د: put the tongue tip against your teeth, as if starting to say 'th'.
For ټ ډ: curl the tongue tip up and back, then say t/d — the sound becomes 'hollow'.
For ړ: say 'arda' quickly with a curled tongue, and let the d become a flap.
ڼ only appears in the middle or end of words: مڼه maṇá, وروڼه wróṇa.

pronunciation.title: ښ and ږ: the soft and hard dialects
pronunciation.body:
The letters **ښ** and **ږ** are the best-known dialect markers in Pashto. In the **soft** southern dialects (Kandahar) and the standard taught in this course, ښ is a 'curled' sh (ʂ) — say sh with the tongue tip turned up and back — and ږ is its voiced partner, a curled zh (ʐ). In the **hard** northern dialects (Peshawar, Mardan, Swat, Bajaur) ښ is pronounced **x** (like خ) and ږ is pronounced **g**.

That is why the same word is *Pashto* (paṣtó) in Kandahar and *Pakhto* (paxtó) in Peshawar, and why the people are *Pashtun* or *Pakhtun*. Central and eastern Afghan speakers (around Kabul, Ghazni, Paktia) have intermediate pronunciations, such as a palatal 'ç' (like German 'ich') for ښ. All of these are correct and understood everywhere; just be consistent. If you are learning for Peshawar, simply read every ṣ in this course as x and every ẓ as g.
tips: Soft ṣ: start with English 'sh', then curl the tongue tip back — it should sound slightly 'darker'.
Don't merge ښ with ش: ښه ṣə 'good' and شه sha 'become!' are different words.
Peshawar ښار (city) is pronounced xār — the same as خار 'thorn'; context sorts it out.
موږ 'we' is muẓ in Kandahar and mung or mug in Peshawar (spelt مونږ in Pakistan).

pairs.note: Different in Kandahar; identical in Peshawar (both xār).
Both spellings exist — you will meet ش in many loans.
Curled ẓ vs ordinary zh (Peshawar: gira vs zhaṛā).

pronunciation.title: The throat sounds خ x, غ ġ and ق q
pronunciation.body:
**خ (x)** is the rough sound in Scottish 'loch' or German 'Bach': raise the back of the tongue towards the soft palate and push air through without closing. **غ (ġ)** is the same position with the voice on — a gargled sound close to the French or German r. Both are very common in native Pashto words (غر ġar 'mountain', خور xor 'sister', غوښه ġwáṣa 'meat').

**ق (q)** is a k made even further back, against the uvula. It occurs in Arabic loans; many Pashto speakers simply say k, so don't worry too much about it. What *does* matter is keeping خ and غ distinct from ک and ګ.
tips: Say 'k' but don't let the tongue touch the palate — that's x.
Gargle gently with your voice on — that's ġ.
Never write or say kh for خ; Pashto has no aspirated k.
Practise in pairs: کر kar / خر xar, ګټه gaṭa / غټه ġaṭa.

pairs.note: Not a perfect pair, but practise the onset x vs k.

pronunciation.title: The affricates څ ts and ځ dz
pronunciation.body:
Pashto has two sounds English only has at the ends of words: **څ ts** (as in 'cats') and **ځ dz** (as in 'adze', 'kids'). In Pashto they come at the start of very common words: څه tsə 'what', څوک tsok 'who', څنګه tsənga 'how', ځم dzəm 'I go', ځای dzāy 'place', ځوان dzwān 'young'.

Make them as a single quick sound, not 't' + 's'. Keep them distinct from چ ch and ج j, which are made with the tongue further back. In the Yusufzai (Peshawar/Swat) dialect څ is often just s and ځ just z: څه 'what' sounds like 'sa'.
tips: Say 'cats', then drop the 'ca' — the 'ts' left over is څ.
Say 'kids', drop the 'ki' — the 'dz' is ځ.
Don't add a vowel before: ځم is one syllable, dzəm.

pronunciation.title: Short a, long ā and the schwa ə
pronunciation.body:
Pashto has three 'a-like' vowels, and confusing them changes words. **ā** (written ا) is long and open, often slightly rounded towards the 'aw' of 'law'. **a** is short and central, like the u in 'cup'. **ə** is the shortest and most neutral, the 'uh' in 'about' or the a in 'sofa'.

The schwa ə is everywhere — in the tiny grammar words زه zə 'I', ته tə 'you', په pə 'in', د də 'of', نه nə — but it is rarely written inside a word. At the end of a word **ه** can be either **-ə** (زه zə, زړه zṛə) or **-a** (feminine nouns: ښځه ṣədzá, مڼه maṇá). The same written word can therefore be two words: زړه is zṛə 'heart' or zaṛa 'old (f)'.
tips: Keep ə really short and lazy — never a full 'ah'.
Final -a of feminine nouns is a clear, short 'a'.
If a word ends in ه, check the romanization: -a or -ə?
Long ā is held a little longer than a and has a darker colour.

pairs.note: Same spelling: schwa and cluster vs a-a.

pronunciation.title: The grammatical endings -ay, -i, -e, -əy
pronunciation.body:
The five ye letters at the end of a word are not just spelling: each is a different vowel with a different grammatical meaning, and you have to hear them clearly. **-ay** (ی) is like 'eye' — masculine singular: سړی saṛáy 'man'. **-i** (ي) — masculine plural and the 3rd-person verb ending: سړي saṛí 'men', کوي kawí 'he does'. **-e** (ې) as in 'café' — feminine and 2nd-person singular: ستړې stə́ṛe 'tired (f)', ځې dze 'you go'. **-əy** (ۍ ئ) — feminine -əy nouns and the 2nd-person plural verb: نجلۍ njlə́y 'girl', ځئ dzəy 'you (pl.) go'.

Saying -ay instead of -i turns 'men' into 'man'; saying -e instead of -əy changes 'you (one person)' into 'you (polite/plural)'. Practise the endings in pairs until they feel distinct.
tips: -ay: open your mouth wide then glide to y; -əy: start from a lazy 'uh'.
-e is a pure vowel, without the y-glide English adds in 'day'.
When you speak to an elder, listen for -əy: کېنئ kénəy 'please sit'.

drill.native: زه ځم، ته ځې، هغه ځي
drill.roman: zə dzəm, tə dze, haġá dzi
drill.en: I go, you go, he goes

pronunciation.title: Stress changes meaning
pronunciation.body:
Pashto stress is free: it can fall on different syllables, and moving it can change the meaning — especially in verbs. The clearest case is **aspect**. In the past tense the imperfective ('was doing') is usually stressed at the end, while the perfective ('did') is stressed at the beginning, on the prefix **wə́-** or on a verb prefix such as rā́-, préwat-, kén-. Some verbs look identical in writing and differ **only** in stress.

In nouns, stress is mostly on the last syllable of the stem (saṛáy, kitā́b, ṣədzá), but there are many exceptions (óṛay 'summer', mánay 'autumn', ẓíra 'beard'). This course marks stress with an accent wherever it matters; copy what you hear from native speakers.
tips: Always stress the perfective prefix: wə́kṛa 'do (it)!', wə́xwaṛa 'he ate'.
Say the pairs below with a clear beat: rāwṛə́m (…ṚƏM) vs rā́wṛəm (RĀ…).
Don't reduce unstressed vowels the English way — ā stays ā.

pairs.note: Imperfective vs perfective: only the stress differs.
Here the two aspects even use different stems.

pronunciation.title: Consonant clusters at the start of words
pronunciation.body:
Many Pashto words begin with two (or even three) consonants: **ښځه** ṣədzá, **ستړی** stə́ṛay, **لمر** lmar 'sun', **پلار** plār, **ورور** wror, **ښکلی** ṣkə́lay, **سپين** spin. Speakers of Urdu, Persian and many Indian languages tend to break these up with an extra vowel ('ispin', 'sitaṛay') — native speakers notice immediately.

English speakers have an advantage with s- clusters (spin, star), but unfamiliar ones like lm-, zṛ-, ṣk-, dr-, pṣ-, wr-, mẓ- need practice. Glide straight from the first consonant into the second; don't insert a vowel in front or between.
tips: Say lmar as 'l' + 'mar' joined with no vowel: hum the l into the m.
Use 'spin' and 'school' as models for سپين spin and ښکلی ṣkə́lay.
Whisper the cluster first, then add the voice.

pronunciation.title: No puff of air: p, t, k and dental t, d
pronunciation.body:
English p, t, k at the start of a word are **aspirated** — they come with a puff of air (hold your hand in front of your mouth and say 'pin'). Pashto p, t, k never have this puff: they sound like the p in 'spin', the t in 'stop', the k in 'skin'. Pashto also has **no aspirated consonants at all** (unlike Urdu and Hindi), so in Urdu loanwords the h is dropped or the word is adapted.

At the same time, remember that ت and د are **dental**: the tongue tip touches the upper teeth. An English t in 'tea' is both aspirated and alveolar, so Pashto ت in تور tor 'black' should sound sharper and 'cleaner'.
tips: Hold a sheet of paper in front of your lips: it should not move when you say پلار plār.
Pretend there is an s before the word: (s)pin → پ, (s)kin → ک.
Tongue on the teeth for ت د, curled back for ټ ډ.

pronunciation.title: Arabic letters: several letters, one sound
pronunciation.body:
Pashto has borrowed many words from Arabic (often via Persian), and kept their spelling. As a result several letters are pronounced the same: **ث س ص** are all *s*; **ذ ز ض ظ** are all *z*; **ت ط** are both *t*; **ه ح** are both *h*. **ع** and **ء** are usually silent or just a small catch between vowels.

So you only need to learn one sound for each group — but you do have to learn spellings word by word, just as English speakers learn 'night' and 'knight'.
tips: Don't try to make Arabic 'emphatic' sounds — Pashto speakers don't.
ع at the start of a word is just the vowel: علم ilm (written ʿilm in this course).
Learn the common loans as whole words: صحت sihát 'health', ضرور zarúr 'certainly'.

pronunciation.title: و is w, not v; ف and the p tendency
pronunciation.body:
Pashto **و** is a real **w**, made with rounded lips, as in English 'we': ورور wror 'brother', ونه wə́na 'tree', وخت waxt 'time'. Urdu and Persian speakers often say v; in Pashto that sounds foreign. After a consonant, و often makes a cluster: خوږ xwaẓ 'sweet', دوه dwa 'two', غوښه ġwáṣa 'meat'.

**ف f** exists in loanwords (فکر fikr, فوټبال fuṭbā́l), but in many rural varieties it is replaced by p. You will hear both; use f.
tips: Round your lips for و — never touch teeth to lip.
In xw-, dw-, ġw- clusters, start rounding your lips before the first consonant.

pairs.note: و as vowel o vs consonant w.

pronunciation.title: Asking yes/no questions with intonation
pronunciation.body:
Pashto has no special word for turning a statement into a yes/no question (no 'do' or 'est-ce que'): you simply **raise your voice at the end**. ته ستړی يې. 'You are tired.' — falling; ته ستړی يې؟ 'Are you tired?' — rising on the last word.

Questions with question words (څه what, څوک who, چېرته where) usually fall at the end, like English 'What's your name?'. Pashto speakers also often add **نه؟** na? at the end, like English 'isn't it?'.
tips: Yes/no question: a clear rise on the final word.
Wh-question: start high on the question word, fall at the end.
Add 'nə?' to ask for confirmation: ښه ده، نه؟
